item.title: “O brahmin, strive to cut the stream, Abandon sensual pleasures. Knowing the destruction of formations, You will be the one who knows the Unmade.” “By…
item.description:
“O brahmin, strive to cut the stream,
Abandon sensual pleasures.
Knowing the destruction of formations,
You will be the one who knows the Unmade.”

“By always dwelling in two Dhammas,
One reaches the further shore.
That brahmin, wise,
Cuts off all fetters.”

“One who has no near shore, no far shore,
No both shores,
Free from suffering, unbound —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“Meditating, free from dust,
Duty done, without defilements,
Having attained the highest goal —
Him I call a brahmin.”

From: Dhammapada 383-423

item.title: “Rādha, whatever is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Rādha, is suffering? The eye, Rādha, is suffering — there you should…
item.description:
“Rādha, whatever is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Rādha, is suffering? The eye, Rādha, is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Forms … Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact … that feeling is suffering. There you should abandon your desire. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind … Phenomena … Mind-consciousness … Mind-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact … that feeling is suffering. There you should abandon your desire. Whatever is suffering, Rādha — there you should abandon your desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.77

item.title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied, infatuated, or utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who see their peril, who…
item.description:
“Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied, infatuated, or utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who see their peril, who know the escape from them, and who enjoy them—they should be understood as not fallen into misfortune, not fallen into calamity, and are not being used by Māra as he wishes. Monks, just as a forest deer that has not fallen into a trap does not have to lie down—that deer should be understood as not fallen into misfortune, not fallen into calamity, and is not being used by the hunter as he wishes. When the hunter comes, the deer can leave as it wishes. So too, monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied … are not being used by Māra as he wishes.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant feeling, monks, should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant feeling, monks, should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should be seen as a dart. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be seen as impermanent. When, monks, a monk sees pleasant feeling as suffering, sees painful feeling as a dart, sees neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent — then, monks, he is called a monk who has right view, who has cut off craving, who has destroyed the fetters. By thoroughly breaking through conceit, he has made an end of suffering.

One who sees pleasure as suffering,
And sees pain as a dart,
Sees the neutral feeling
As impermanent —
That monk sees rightly,
Fully understanding feelings.

Having fully understood feelings,
He is defilement-free in this very life.
At the breaking of the body, that Dhamma-abider,
The great sage, is beyond measure.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.5

item.title: “Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with…
item.description:
“Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … with feeling … with perception … with formations … with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, knowledge arises: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’

Happy indeed are the arahants,
In them no craving is found,
Conceit has been cut off,
The net of delusion is torn apart.

They have attained the imperturbable,
Their minds are far from defilement,
They are not stained in the world —
The holy ones, free from defilements.

Fully understanding the five aggregates,
Practicing the seven good qualities,
Praised by true persons,
Disciples of the Buddha.

Possessing seven treasures,
Completed in the three trainings,
The great heroes wander forth,
Having abandoned all fear.

Endowed with ten powers,
The great elephant is concentrated,
They are supreme in the world,
Craving has been destroyed.

Achieved the knowledge of the adept,
This body is their last,
The end of the holy life,
Achieved independently.

Not shaken by perceptions,
Liberated from renewed existence,
Having reached the tamed state,
They are conquerors in the world.

Above, below, and across,
They have no delight,
They roar the lion’s roar —
The supreme Buddhas in the world!

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.76

item.title: “Monks, on King Snowy Mountain there are rough, uneven stretches where neither monkeys nor humans go. On King Snowy Mountain there are rough, uneven stretches…
item.description:
“Monks, on King Snowy Mountain there are rough, uneven stretches where neither monkeys nor humans go. On King Snowy Mountain there are rough, uneven stretches where monkeys go but humans do not. On King Snowy Mountain there are even, pleasant stretches where both monkeys and humans go. There, monks, hunters set a trap of sticky resin on the paths where monkeys go, to catch monkeys. Here, monks, those monkeys that are not foolish and not greedy avoid the trap of resin when they see it. But a foolish, greedy monkey, seeing the resin, reaches out with its hand and gets stuck. Wanting to free its hand, it reaches out with the other hand and gets stuck. Wanting to free both hands, it reaches out with one foot and gets stuck. Wanting to free its hands and foot, it reaches out with the other foot and gets stuck. Wanting to free its hands and feet, it puts its mouth to it and gets stuck. Thus, monks, the monkey, caught in five places, lies down screeching, having fallen into misfortune, into calamity, subject to the hunter’s will. The hunter then kills it, roasts it over a charcoal fire, and goes away as he wishes. So too, monks, for one who wanders outside his own proper range, into the domain of others. For one who wanders outside his proper range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.7

item.title: “Mahānāma, in the past, when I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I saw with correct wisdom as it actually is: ‘Sensual pleasures…
item.description:
“Mahānāma, in the past, when I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I saw with correct wisdom as it actually is: ‘Sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Yet, even though I saw that with correct wisdom, I did not attain the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, of non-sensuality, of unwholesome states, or anything higher than that. And then I knew that I was not yet free from being dominated by sensual pleasures. Mahānāma, when I saw with correct wisdom as it actually is: ‘Sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater,’ and I attained the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, of non-sensuality, of unwholesome states, or anything higher than that, then I knew that I was free from being dominated by sensual pleasures.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 14 – Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasutta

item.title: “Good sirs, what is the pursuit of the past? ‘My eye in the past was such and such, forms were such and such, and consciousness…
item.description:
“Good sirs, what is the pursuit of the past? ‘My eye in the past was such and such, forms were such and such, and consciousness there was bound by desire and lust. Because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, he delights in that. Delighting in that, he pursues the past. My ear in the past … nose … tongue … body … mind in the past was such and such, phenomena were such and such, and consciousness there was bound by desire and lust. Because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, he delights in that. Delighting in that, he pursues the past.’ This, good sirs, is the pursuit of the past.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 133 – Mahākaccānabhaddekarattasutta

item.title: “Monks, if that monk, while examining the peril in those thoughts, still has evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion arising, then that…
item.description:
“Monks, if that monk, while examining the peril in those thoughts, still has evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion arising, then that monk should not attend to, not give attention to those thoughts. By not attending to, not giving attention to those thoughts, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, the mind becomes steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated. Monks, just as a person with eyes, not wanting to see forms within his range, would close his eyes or look away; so too, monks, that monk, by not attending … the mind becomes steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 20 – Vitakkasaṇṭhānasutta

item.title: “Monks, the arising, the continuation, the production, the manifestation of the eye is the arising of suffering, the continuation of disease, the manifestation of aging…
item.description:
“Monks, the arising, the continuation, the production, the manifestation of the eye is the arising of suffering, the continuation of disease, the manifestation of aging and death. The arising … of the ear … of the nose … of the tongue … of the body … of the mind is the arising of suffering, the continuation of disease, the manifestation of aging and death. The cessation, the stilling, the ending of the eye is the cessation of suffering, the stilling of disease, the ending of aging and death. The cessation … of the ear … of the nose … of the tongue … of the body … of the mind is the cessation of suffering, the stilling of disease, the ending of aging and death.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 26.1
